steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
Domain generalization setting and goal
- learning theory usually assumes identically distributed data
- domain generalization: N\in\mathbb{N} samples from N different distributions P^{(1)},\ldots,P^{(N)} (domains, e.g. different medical patients)
- goal: model g:(x_{i}^{T})_{i=1}^{n}\mapsto(\widehat{f}:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Y}), predictor from unlabeled target data (x_{i}^{T})_{i=1}^{n}\in\mathcal{X}^{n} of new P^{T}
- performance \mathcal{E}^{\infty}(g):=\int\int(\widehat{f}(x)-y)^{2}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}P^{T}(x,y)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}E(P^{T}), meta-distribution / environment E

Question: worst-case sample complexity
- this work: worst-case sample complexity of domain generalization
- can g be computed from the N samples with small bounds on \mathcal{E}^{\infty}(g)-\inf_{h}\mathcal{E}^{\infty}(h), and how?

Prior work: meta-learning, multi-task, marginal transfer; no rates
- many finite sample results in meta-learning, multi-task learning; less for domain generalization
- target labels inaccessible -> new techniques needed
- must relate marginal P_{\mathcal{X}}^{T}(x) to conditional P^{T}(y|x), P^{T}(x,y)=P_{\mathcal{X}}^{T}(x)P^{T}(y|x)
- done implicitly in marginal transfer approach: universal consistent algorithm, \mathcal{E}^{\infty}(g)\to\inf_{h}\mathcal{E}^{\infty}(h) a.s. for n,N\to\infty
- rate of convergence still open

Our idea: domain generalization as functional regression
- main conceptual contribution: recast domain generalization as functional regression -> analytical results from that field
- new algorithm: learn operator mapping (kernel mean embeddings of) marginals P_{\mathcal{X}}(x) to approximations of regression functions (Bayes predictors) f_{P}:=\argmin_{f:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Y}}\int_{\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}}(f(x)-y)^{2}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}P(x,y) of conditionals P(y|x)
- first step: linear operator, slope functions in an RKHS -> existing analytical arguments -> explicit finite sample bounds
- opens directions: linear and non-linear operator learning

Practical advantage: different RKHSs per domain
- can choose different reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces (RKHSs) for regression on different source distributions (P^{(i)})_{i=1}^{N}
- allows expert choices and automation, e.g. cross-validation over well-known kernels
- numerical example illustrating this, simple implementation

Contributions
- new concept: domain generalization by functional regression
- new algorithm, domain-specific data-based predictors (different learned RKHSs per domain); target predictors need not be approximable by pre-defined (e.g. Gaussian) RKHSs
- first finite sample bounds for \mathcal{E}^{\infty}(g)-\inf_{h}\mathcal{E}^{\infty}(h) in this setting
- numerical implementation showing the advantage

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
In learning theory most problems assume that the data is identically distributed. In domain generalization this is not the case: the learner observes N\in\mathbb{N} data samples, and they follow N different distributions P^{(1)},\ldots,P^{(N)}. The source distributions model different real-world domains, for example different medical patients. In domain generalization the goal is to find a model g:(x_{i}^{T})_{i=1}^{n}\mapsto(\widehat{f}:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Y}) which can derive a predictor \widehat{f}:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Y} only from unlabeled data (x_{i}^{T})_{i=1}^{n}\in\mathcal{X}^{n} that follows a new target distribution P^{T}. How well g performs is measured in expectation over a random draw of the target distribution P^{T}, that is by \mathcal{E}^{\infty}(g):=\int\int(\widehat{f}(x)-y)^{2}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}P^{T}(x,y)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}E(P^{T}), where E is some meta-distribution (or environment) that P^{T} is drawn from.

The topic of this work is the worst-case sample complexity of domain generalization. To be more precise, the question we study is whether and how the model g above can be computed from the N given samples so that it satisfies small bounds on \mathcal{E}^{\infty}(g)-\inf_{h}\mathcal{E}^{\infty}(h)?

There are many finite sample results in the similar settings of meta-learning (see e.g.) and multi-task learning (see e.g.), but less is known for domain generalization. The reason is that target labels are not accessible, so domain generalization needs new techniques. For example, if we want to learn from unlabeled data of a target distribution P^{T}, we have to relate the marginal distribution P_{\mathcal{X}}^{T}(x) (of inputs x\in\mathcal{X}) to the conditional distribution P^{T}(y|x) (of outputs y\in\mathcal{Y} w.r.t. inputs), where P^{T}(x,y)=P_{\mathcal{X}}^{T}(x)P^{T}(y|x). This is done implicitly in the seminal marginal transfer approach, which proposes a universal consistent algorithm, i.e. an algorithm that computes g such that \mathcal{E}^{\infty}(g)\to\inf_{h}\mathcal{E}^{\infty}(h) almost surely for n,N\to\infty. But as far as we know, the rate of this convergence is still an open research problem.

The main conceptual contribution of this work is that we recast domain generalization as a functional regression problem, so that analytical results from that field can be used. More precisely, we propose a new algorithm that explicitly learns (from the input samples) an operator, and this operator maps (kernel mean embeddings of) input marginal distributions P_{\mathcal{X}}(x) to approximations of the regression functions (Bayes predictors) f_{P}:=\argmin_{f:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Y}}\int_{\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}}(f(x)-y)^{2}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}P(x,y) of the corresponding conditional distributions P(y|x). As a first step, we focus here on learning a linear operator with slope functions in an RKHS, which lets us use analytical arguments from earlier work and gives explicit finite sample bounds. But the new concept also opens new directions for domain generalization by linear and non-linear operator learning.

Another advantage of our method, which is especially practical, is that we can choose different reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces (RKHSs) for regression on different source distributions (P^{(i)})_{i=1}^{N}. This allows expert-choices and also automation, for example choosing between well-known kernels by cross-validation. We give a numerical example that illustrates this advantage and gives a simple implementation of the algorithm. Our contributions are summarized as follows:

- We give a new concept for domain generalization, which approaches it by functional regression.

- We propose a new algorithm that allows predictors to be constructed in a domain-specific, data-based way, for example with different learned RKHSs for different domains. One consequence is that new target predictors do not need to be well approximable by pre-defined (e.g. Gaussian) RKHSs.

- We give finite sample bounds for \mathcal{E}^{\infty}(g)-\inf_{h}\mathcal{E}^{\infty}(h) in the domain generalization setting, which to our knowledge are the first ones.

- We give a numerical implementation that shows the advantage of our algorithm.

- We give a new concept for domain generalization, which approaches it by functional regression.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Most problems in learning theory assume that data is identically distributed. In contrast, in domain generalization [1,2,3], the learner observes N\in\mathbb{N} data samples

which follow N different distributions P^{(1)},\ldots,P^{(N)}. The source distributions model different real-world domains, e.g., different medical patients. The goal of domain generalization is to find a model g:(x_{i}^{T})_{i=1}^{n}\mapsto(\widehat{f}:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Y}) that is able to derive a predictor \widehat{f}:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Y} from only unlabeled data (x_{i}^{T})_{i=1}^{n}\in\mathcal{X}^{n} following a new target distribution P^{T}. The performance of g is quantified in expectation over a random draw of the target distribution P^{T}, i.e., by \mathcal{E}^{\infty}(g):=\int\int(\widehat{f}(x)-y)^{2}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}P^{T}(x,y)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}E(P^{T}) for some meta-distribution (or environment [4]) E from which P^{T} is drawn.

This work studies the worst-case sample complexity of domain generalization. More precisely, we study the question of whether and how the model g above can be computed from the N given samples, such that it satisfies small bounds on \mathcal{E}^{\infty}(g)-\inf_{h}\mathcal{E}^{\infty}(h) ?

Although many finite sample results are available in the similar settings of meta-learning (cf. [5]) and multi-task learning (cf. [6]), less is known for domain generalization. The inaccessibility of target labels requires new techniques for domain generalization. For example, to learn from unlabeled data of a target distribution P^{T}, it is required to relate the marginal distribution P_{\mathcal{X}}^{T}(x) (of inputs x\in\mathcal{X}) to the conditional distribution P^{T}(y|x) (of outputs y\in\mathcal{Y} w.r.t. inputs), where P^{T}(x,y)=P_{\mathcal{X}}^{T}(x)P^{T}(y|x). This is implicitly done in the seminal marginal transfer approach of [1,3], where a universal consistent algorithm is proposed, i.e., an algorithm computing g such that \mathcal{E}^{\infty}(g)\to\inf_{h}\mathcal{E}^{\infty}(h) almost surely for n,N\to\infty. However, to the best of our knowledge, specifying the rate of this convergence is still an open research problem.

The main conceptual contribution of this work is to recast domain generalization as a problem of functional regression, which allows for analytical results from that field. More precisely, we propose a new algorithm for explicitly learning (from the input samples) an operator, which maps (kernel mean embeddings of) input marginal distributions P_{\mathcal{X}}(x) to approximations of the regression functions (Bayes predictors) f_{P}:=\argmin_{f:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Y}}\int_{\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}}(f(x)-y)^{2}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}P(x,y) of the corresponding conditional distributions P(y|x). Here, as a first step, we focus on learning a linear operator with slope functions residing in an RKHS, which allows us to apply analytical arguments from [7,8,9] resulting in explicit finite sample bounds. However, our new concept opens new directions for domain generalization by linear and non-linear operator learning.

Another practical advantage of our method is the possibility to choose different reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces (RKHSs) for regression on different source distributions (P^{(i)})_{i=1}^{N}. This allows expert-choices and automation, e.g., by choosing between well-known kernels by cross-validation. We provide a numerical example which illustrates this advantage and gives a simple implementation of the proposed algorithm. Our contributions can be summarized as follows:

- • We provide a new concept for approaching domain generalization by functional regression.

- • We propose a new algorithm which allows a domain-specific data-based construction of predictors, e.g., different learned RKHSs for different domains. As one consequence, new target predictors are not needed to be well approximable by pre-defined (e.g. Gaussian) RKHSs.

- • We provide (to the best of our knowledge first) finite sample bounds for \mathcal{E}^{\infty}(g)-\inf_{h}\mathcal{E}^{\infty}(h) in the domain generalization setting of [1].

- • We provide a numerical implementation which shows the advantage of our algorithm.

[2] Muandet et al. [2013] K. Muandet, D. Balduzzi, and B. Schölkopf. Domain generalization via invariant feature representation. In International Conference on Machine Learning , pages 10–18. PMLR, 2013.
[3] Blanchard et al. [2021] G. Blanchard, A. A. Deshmukh, Ü. Dogan, G. Lee, and C. Scott. Domain generalization by marginal transfer learning. The Journal of Machine Learning Research , 22(1):46–100, 2021.
